analysis.one_liner: Moves spent nuclear fuel from reactor sites to a Nevada storage facility and shields the government from missed-deadline lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed it 65-34 on April 15, 1997, but the House never voted and it died when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Energy Department to build an interim storage facility at the Nevada Test Site and start hauling spent nuclear fuel away from civilian reactor sites shortly after licensing, with money payments and land giveaways to nearby Nevada counties. It would have overridden Nevada state and local law, narrowed the environmental review of the site, and barred the government from being sued over missed waste-acceptance deadlines. The Senate passed it, but the House never took it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Nuclear utilities that hold Department of Energy waste contracts gain the most: the bill puts a firm clock on federal acceptance of their spent fuel, promises reimbursement for transportable storage systems they bought, and pays for storage of fuel at one specific reactor. The rail, trucking, and cask manufacturers who would build and run the shipment system also gain, because the bill requires the waste to be moved and the equipment to be American-made.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nuclear utilities holding DOE waste contracts

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Secretary of Energy to begin storing the utilities' spent nuclear fuel at a Nevada interim facility no later than 18 months after the storage facility is licensed, ending the open-ended wait utilities have faced since DOE missed its 1998 acceptance deadline.

Requires DOE to consent to reimburse contract holders for transportable storage systems they purchased, and authorizes DOE to accept all spent fuel from Dairyland Power's La Crosse reactor and pay for its on-site storage until removal.

Designates a specific site in Area 25 of the Nevada Test Site for the interim facility and deems it approved by law if the President or Congress fails to act within set deadlines, so the project cannot be blocked by further process.

Protects utilities' existing waste contract rights and the federal court order requiring DOE to accept waste, while directing DOE to run the program 'to the maximum extent possible' through private sector contracting.

analysis.who_pays: Nevada would host the interim facility at the Nevada Test Site and absorb the risk of tens of thousands of waste shipments crossing dozens of states, while the bill preempts Nevada's state and local laws and cuts short the environmental review that would have weighed alternative sites or the need for the project at all. The federal liability shield would leave taxpayers and waste-fee payers without recourse if the government missed its deadlines again. Electricity customers already pay the nuclear waste fee that funds the program.
analysis.who_pays_short: Nevada residents and communities along shipping routes

drawbacks.text: The bill exempts the siting and preliminary decisions from full environmental impact statements and bars the final review from considering alternatives to geological disposal or interim storage, or any site other than the one chosen for Nevada.

It sets the repository radiation standard at a lifetime cancer death risk of up to about 1 in 1,000 for the most exposed group, and instructs regulators not to consider human intrusion into the repository or climate regimes different from the last 100,000 years.

It preempts state and local law and gives federal appeals courts exclusive jurisdiction over lawsuits, leaving Nevada and communities along the shipping routes little legal standing to challenge the facility or the shipments.

It shields the United States from financial liability if the Secretary of Energy again fails to meet acceptance or emplacement deadlines, so waste-fee payers and utilities would have no claim for the next missed schedule.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real problem — spent fuel stranded at reactor sites because DOE missed its contractual acceptance deadline — and it included genuine safety provisions, such as banning shipments through a jurisdiction until emergency-response training is complete and funding worker health and safety training. But its core bargain was one-sided: it forced a facility and thousands of shipments on Nevada over the state's objection, preempted state authority, curtailed the environmental review of alternatives, capped the radiation standard's scope, and removed the legal remedy for future missed deadlines. The speed for utilities came at the expense of the state and communities the waste would pass through.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it 65-34 on April 15, 1997, but the House never voted; the bill sat at the House desk and died when the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, chaired by the bill's sponsor, held hearings in February 1997, amended and reported the bill in March, and placed it on the calendar.
Several attempts to start floor debate stalled in March 1997, with cloture motions on the motion to proceed filed and then withdrawn, before the Senate took the bill up in April.
The Senate passed the amended bill on April 15, 1997, by a vote of 65 to 34 — 53 of 55 Republicans and 12 of 45 Democrats in favor, with 32 Democrats and 2 Republicans opposed.
The House received the bill on April 16, 1997, and held it at the desk; no vote was ever scheduled, and in March 1998 the papers were returned to the Senate.

The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, with the bill never enacted, so the federal government never began the Nevada interim storage program and remained liable under existing contracts for its missed waste-acceptance deadlines.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nevada and the communities along the proposed shipping routes are better off, because the interim facility was never built and the waste never moved. Nuclear utilities are worse off in the short run — their fuel stayed on site — though they later pursued damages claims for DOE's missed deadlines instead.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nevada and communities along the shipping routes

for.name: Sen. Frank Murkowski
for.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, chaired the hearings, managed it through committee, reported it to the floor, and steered it to Senate passage.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a vote; the bill was held at the House desk from April 1997 until the papers were returned to the Senate in March 1998.

against.name: Nevada's senators, Harry Reid and Richard Bryan
against.what_they_did: Led opposition to forcing an interim waste facility and waste shipments on Nevada over the state's objection.

against.name: President Clinton
against.what_they_did: Threatened to veto the interim storage legislation, which mattered because the 65-34 Senate total fell short of the 67 votes needed to override.

sides.party_line_note: The Senate split mostly by party: 53 of 55 Republicans voted yes along with 12 of 45 Democrats, while opposition was 32 of 45 Democrats plus 2 Republicans.

industries.note: The bill set a firm deadline for the federal government to take the utilities' spent fuel off their hands, preserved their contract rights, and promised reimbursement for storage systems they bought — solving a problem that has cost them and their ratepayers. But the gain came by shifting the facility, the shipments, and the legal risk onto Nevada and the transport corridors.

industries.industry: Radioactive waste transport and cask manufacturers
industries.note: The bill required DOE to procure transport systems and mandated that the equipment be manufactured in the United States, creating a large guaranteed procurement program and steady shipping campaigns by rail and heavy-haul truck.

The bill directed the NRC to establish licensing procedures for dry storage technology without site-specific approvals to the maximum extent possible, easing the path for expanded on-site storage until federal pickup.

Customers of nuclear utilities had paid a fee on every kilowatt-hour into the Nuclear Waste Fund on the promise of disposal. The bill continued the fee and shielded the government from liability for missing deadlines, leaving fee payers without recourse for further delays.
